claims.text: A questionnaire can collect comparable answers from many respondents at manageable cost, and a self-completed form may reduce interviewer pressure. Closed choices can hide reasons, unclear wording can distort answers, and low literacy or non-response can exclude people. Interviews allow clarification and detailed explanations, but take more time and can be affected by leading questions or pressure to please the interviewer. Observation records visible conditions directly and can use repeatable categories, but it cannot establish private motives; unusual times or weather can distort a short visit. Secondary evidence saves collection time and may supply wider or historical comparisons, but dates, units, definitions or coverage may not fit the enquiry. Compare at least two relevant benefits and limitations when choosing; do not substitute a definition of the method for its evaluation.

claims.text: This demonstration is invented, not an enquiry you carried out. Suppose a safe observation found 12 visible items at one site and six at another during the same period, with one route inaccessible. The finding is a two-to-one count contrast in the observed places, not a result for the whole community. A conclusion can say the recorded sites differed, while noting missing coverage. A recommendation might ask the responsible collection provider to inspect the higher-count site. For your own answer, replace the demonstration with your actual observations and limits. Do not claim these counts, visits or recommendations as your own experience.
